Q781 --- Complete solution
\begin{enumerate}

Let \$G\$ be a compact topological group, and let \$\(A_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}\$ be a family of subsets of \$G\$. The family is called separable by translations if there are elements \$t\_i\textbackslash{}in G\$ such that the left translates \$t\_iA\_i\$, \$i\textbackslash{}in I\$, are pairwise disjoint.
Given a family \$\(U_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}\$ of open subsets of \$G\$, assume that every finite subfamily is separable by translations. Prove that the whole family is separable by translations.
The PDF first says merely ``let \$G\$ be a group'' and then speaks of compactness and open subsets. The intended meaning must therefore be ``compact topological group.'' The word ``separable'' is the specially defined translation-packing property, not separability in the sense of possessing a countable dense subset. \begin{enumerate}
\item The theorem
\end{enumerate}
Theorem
Let \$G\$ be a compact topological group, let \$I\$ be an arbitrary index set, and let \$U\_i\textbackslash{}subseteq G\$ be open for every \$i\textbackslash{}in I\$. Suppose that for every finite \$F\textbackslash{}subseteq I\$, there exist elements \$t\_i\textasciicircum{}\{\(F\)\}\textbackslash{}in G\$, \$i\textbackslash{}in F\$, such that

\$\$
t\_i\textasciicircum{}\{\(F\)\}U\_i\textbackslash{}cap t\_j\textasciicircum{}\{\(F\)\}U\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing
\textbackslash{}qquad\(i,j\in F,\ i\neq j\).
\$\$

Then there exist elements \$t\_i\textbackslash{}in G\$, \$i\textbackslash{}in I\$, such that

\$\$
t\_iU\_i\textbackslash{}cap t\_jU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing
\textbackslash{}qquad\(i,j\in I,\ i\neq j\).
\$\$

Thus Q781 has an affirmative answer in its full stated generality: neither metrizability of \$G\$ nor countability of \$I\$ is needed.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The disjointness condition is closed
\end{enumerate}
The crucial point is that, because the \$U\_i\$ are open, collision of two translated sets is an open condition on the two translation parameters.
Fix distinct \$i,j\textbackslash{}in I\$. Define

\$\$
R\_\{ij\}
=
\textbackslash{}bigl\textbackslash{}\{(s,t)\textbackslash{}in G\textbackslash{}times G:\textbackslash{} sU\_i\textbackslash{}cap tU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing\textbackslash{}bigr\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

We claim that \$R\_\{ij\}\$ is closed in \$G\textbackslash{}times G\$.
Indeed, for \$s,t\textbackslash{}in G\$,

\$\$
\textbackslash{}begin\{aligned\}
sU\_i\textbackslash{}cap tU\_j\textbackslash{}neq\textbackslash{}varnothing
\&\textbackslash{}iff
\textbackslash{}exists\textbackslash{},u\textbackslash{}in U\_i,\textbackslash{} v\textbackslash{}in U\_j\textbackslash{}text\{ such that \}su=tv\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}
\&\textbackslash{}iff
\textbackslash{}exists\textbackslash{},u\textbackslash{}in U\_i,\textbackslash{} v\textbackslash{}in U\_j\textbackslash{}text\{ such that \}s\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}t=uv\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}
\&\textbackslash{}iff
s\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}t\textbackslash{}in U\_iU\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}.
\textbackslash{}end\{aligned\}
\$\$

The subset \$U\_iU\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\$ is open. To see this, inversion is a homeomorphism, so \$U\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\$ is open, and

\$\$
U\_iU\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}
=
\textbackslash{}bigcup\_\{u\textbackslash{}in U\_i\}uU\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}
\$\$

is a union of open left translates.
The map

\$\$
q:G\textbackslash{}times G\textbackslash{}longrightarrow G,
\textbackslash{}qquad
q(s,t)=s\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}t,
\$\$

is continuous. Consequently,

\$\$
\(G\times G\)\textbackslash{}setminus R\_\{ij\}
=
q\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\(U_iU_j^{-1}\)
\$\$

is open. Hence \$R\_\{ij\}\$ is closed.
Notice the useful direction of semicontinuity here: a limit of pairs of translations whose corresponding open sets are disjoint still gives disjoint open sets. In contrast, a limit of intersecting translated open sets need not remain intersecting.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Compactness of the full parameter space
\end{enumerate}
Consider the product space

\$\$
X=G\textasciicircum{}I=\textbackslash{}prod\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}G
\$\$

with the product topology. A point \$x\textbackslash{}in X\$ will be written

\$\$
x=\(x_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}.
\$\$

By Tychonoff's theorem, \$X\$ is compact.
For every unordered pair \$\textbackslash{}\{i,j\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}subseteq I\$, \$i\textbackslash{}neq j\$, define

\$\$
K\_\{ij\}
=
\textbackslash{}bigl\textbackslash{}\{x=\(x_k\)\_\{k\textbackslash{}in I\}\textbackslash{}in X:
x\_iU\_i\textbackslash{}cap x\_jU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing\textbackslash{}bigr\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

Let

\$\$
p\_\{ij\}:X\textbackslash{}longrightarrow G\textbackslash{}times G,
\textbackslash{}qquad
p\_\{ij\}\(x\)=\(x_i,x_j\)
\$\$

be the coordinate projection. Then

\$\$
K\_\{ij\}=p\_\{ij\}\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\(R_{ij}\).
\$\$

Since \$R\_\{ij\}\$ is closed and \$p\_\{ij\}\$ is continuous, \$K\_\{ij\}\$ is closed in \$X\$.
We now prove that the family

\$\$
\textbackslash{}\{K\_\{ij\}:i,j\textbackslash{}in I,\textbackslash{} i\textbackslash{}neq j\textbackslash{}\}
\$\$

has the finite-intersection property.
Take finitely many pair constraints,

\$\$
K\_\{i\_1j\_1\},\textbackslash{}ldots,K\_\{i\_mj\_m\}.
\$\$

Let

\$\$
F=\textbackslash{}\{i\_1,j\_1,\textbackslash{}ldots,i\_m,j\_m\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}subseteq I.
\$\$

This is a finite set of indices. By hypothesis, the finite family \$\(U_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in F\}\$ can be separated: there exist \$s\_i\textbackslash{}in G\$, \$i\textbackslash{}in F\$, such that

\$\$
s\_iU\_i\textbackslash{}cap s\_jU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing
\textbackslash{}qquad\(i,j\in F,\ i\neq j\).
\$\$

Extend this finite assignment to a point \$x\textbackslash{}in G\textasciicircum{}I\$ by setting

\$\$
x\_i=
\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}
s\_i,\&i\textbackslash{}in F,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}
e,\&i\textbackslash{}notin F,
\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
\$\$

where \$e\$ is the identity of \$G\$. Then

\$\$
x\textbackslash{}in K\_\{i\_1j\_1\}\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}cdots\textbackslash{}cap K\_\{i\_mj\_m\}.
\$\$

Thus every finite intersection of the \$K\_\{ij\}\$ is nonempty.
Because \$X\$ is compact and the \$K\_\{ij\}\$ are closed with the finite-intersection property,

\$\$
\textbackslash{}bigcap\_\{\textbackslash{}substack\{i,j\textbackslash{}in I\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}i\textbackslash{}neq j\}\}K\_\{ij\}\textbackslash{}neq\textbackslash{}varnothing.
\$\$

Choose

\$\$
\(t_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}
\textbackslash{}in
\textbackslash{}bigcap\_\{i\textbackslash{}neq j\}K\_\{ij\}.
\$\$

Then, by the definition of \$K\_\{ij\}\$,

\$\$
t\_iU\_i\textbackslash{}cap t\_jU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing
\textbackslash{}qquad\(i\neq j\).
\$\$

Therefore the entire family \$\(U_i\)\_\{i\textbackslash{}in I\}\$ is separable by translations. \(\square\)

\begin{enumerate}
\item The countable metrizable proof
\end{enumerate}
The optional assumptions in the PDF allow a purely sequential formulation.
Suppose \$I=\textbackslash{}mathbb N\$ and \$G\$ is compact metrizable. For each \$n\textbackslash{}geq 1\$, choose translations

\$\$
t\_1\textasciicircum{}\{\(n\)\},\textbackslash{}ldots,t\_n\textasciicircum{}\{\(n\)\}
\$\$

separating \$U\_1,\textbackslash{}ldots,U\_n\$, and extend this to a point \$x\textasciicircum{}\{\(n\)\}\textbackslash{}in G\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}mathbb N\}\$ by setting

\$\$
x\_k\textasciicircum{}\{\(n\)\}=
\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}
t\_k\textasciicircum{}\{\(n\)\},\&k\textbackslash{}leq n,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}
e,\&k>n.
\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
\$\$

If \$d\$ is a compatible metric on \$G\$, the product topology on \$G\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}mathbb N\}\$ is induced by, for example,

\$\$
D(x,y)
=
\textbackslash{}sum\_\{k=1\}\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}infty\}2\textasciicircum{}\{-k\}\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{1,d\(x_k,y_k\)\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

The countable product \$G\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}mathbb N\}\$ is compact metrizable. Equivalently, one may obtain a convergent subsequence by successively extracting subsequences on which the first coordinate converges, then the second, and so on, and taking the diagonal subsequence.
Thus, after passing to a subsequence,

\$\$
x\textasciicircum{}\{\(n_r\)\}\textbackslash{}longrightarrow x=\(t_k\)\_\{k\textbackslash{}geq1\}
\textbackslash{}quad\textbackslash{}text\{in \}G\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}mathbb N\}.
\$\$

Fix \$i\textbackslash{}neq j\$. Since \$n\_r\textbackslash{}to\textbackslash{}infty\$, for every sufficiently large \$r\$,

\$\$
x\_i\textasciicircum{}\{\(n_r\)\}U\_i
\textbackslash{}cap
x\_j\textasciicircum{}\{\(n_r\)\}U\_j
=
\textbackslash{}varnothing.
\$\$

The relation \$R\_\{ij\}\$ proved closed above, so passage to the limit gives

\$\$
t\_iU\_i\textbackslash{}cap t\_jU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing.
\$\$

Since \$i,j\$ were arbitrary, the limit tuple separates the entire family.
Why this is not the general proof
For a general compact group, compactness is not a sequential notion. A compact space need not be sequentially compact, and an uncountable product \$G\textasciicircum{}I\$ generally need not be metrizable or first countable.
For example, the compact Boolean group

\$\$
H=\textbackslash{}\{0,1\textbackslash{}\}\textasciicircum{}\{\textbackslash{}mathcal P\(\mathbb N\)\}
\$\$

is not sequentially compact. Define \$x\_n\textbackslash{}in H\$ by

\$\$
x\_n\(A\)=
\textbackslash{}begin\{cases\}
1,\&n\textbackslash{}in A,\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}
0,\&n\textbackslash{}notin A.
\textbackslash{}end\{cases\}
\$\$

Given any subsequence \$\(x_{n_k}\)\$, take

\$\$
A=\textbackslash{}\{n\_\{2k\}:k\textbackslash{}geq1\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

Then the \$A\$-coordinate of \$x\_\{n\_k\}\$ alternates between \$0\$ and \$1\$, so the subsequence does not converge. Thus a proof that simply says ``extract a convergent subsequence'' would be invalid without the metrizability assumptions. The finite-intersection argument above is genuinely non-sequential and works in the full generality of Q781.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Audit of the topological and set-theoretic assumptions
\end{enumerate}
Separation assumptions
No Hausdorff, regularity, normality, or first-countability axiom is used in the argument itself. The proof only uses:


continuity of multiplication and inversion;


openness of the \$U\_i\$;


compactness of \$G\textasciicircum{}I\$.


Under the usual convention, a ``compact group'' is a compact Hausdorff topological group, but Hausdorffness is not needed for the closed-constraint argument.
Compactness
The general proof uses the arbitrary-product form of Tychonoff's theorem:

The product of an arbitrary family of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.

Compactness is then used through its equivalent finite-intersection formulation: a family of closed subsets of a compact space whose finite intersections are all nonempty has nonempty total intersection.
Countability
No countability assumption on \$I\$ is used. No second-countability or separability assumption on \$G\$ is used.
Countability becomes relevant only if one wishes to replace the product-compactness proof by the sequential diagonal argument.
Choice
In ordinary ZFC, Tychonoff's theorem is available. Foundationally, for compact Hausdorff spaces, the ultrafilter lemma---equivalently the Boolean prime ideal theorem---suffices for the required product compactness; full choice is more than is needed for that step.
No choice is needed to extend a finite tuple to all of \$I\$: the identity \$e\$ supplies a canonical value on every unused coordinate.
In the countable sequential proof, literally choosing one finite separator for every \$n\$ uses a countable selection principle, which is again automatic in ZFC.
The precise role of openness
Openness is used exactly to prove that

\$\$
\textbackslash{}\{(s,t):sU\_i\textbackslash{}cap tU\_j=\textbackslash{}varnothing\textbackslash{}\}
\$\$

is closed. In fact, the same proof works under the weaker pairwise assumption

\$\$
U\_iU\_j\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\textbackslash{} \textbackslash{}text\{is open for every \}i\textbackslash{}neq j.
\$\$

Thus openness of each individual \$U\_i\$ is sufficient but is not the logically weakest possible condition.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Boundary cases
\end{enumerate}
If \$I=\textbackslash{}varnothing\$ or \$|I|=1\$, there are no pairwise constraints, so the conclusion is immediate.
If some \$U\_i=\textbackslash{}varnothing\$, that index causes no constraint because every translate of \$U\_i\$ is empty. Such indices can be ignored and then assigned any translation, for example \$e\$.
If \$G\$ is a finite discrete group of order \$N\$, the hypothesis already implies that there are at most \$N\$ nonempty \$U\_i\$. Indeed, \$N+1\$ pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets cannot exist inside \$G\$. The set of nonempty indices is therefore finite, and applying the hypothesis to that finite subfamily immediately gives the conclusion. This agrees with the general compactness proof.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Why compactness cannot be omitted
\end{enumerate}
The assertion fails for a noncompact group even when:


the group is discrete, metrizable, locally compact, and countable;


\$I\$ is countable;


every \$U\_i\$ is open.


Take

\$\$
G=\(\mathbb Z,+\)
\$\$

with the discrete topology. Let the index set be

\$\$
I=\textbackslash{}\{L,R\textbackslash{}\}\textbackslash{}cup\textbackslash{}mathbb N,
\$\$

and define

\$\$
U\_L=\textbackslash{}\{m\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}mathbb Z:m\textbackslash{}leq0\textbackslash{}\},\textbackslash{}qquad
U\_R=\textbackslash{}\{m\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}mathbb Z:m\textbackslash{}geq0\textbackslash{}\},
\$\$

and

\$\$
U\_n=\textbackslash{}\{0\textbackslash{}\}
\textbackslash{}qquad\(n\in\mathbb N\).
\$\$

Every finite subfamily can be separated. Indeed, suppose it contains \$k\$ of the singleton sets, indexed in some order by \$n\_1,\textbackslash{}ldots,n\_k\$. Use the translations

\$\$
t\_L=0,\textbackslash{}qquad t\_R=k+1,\textbackslash{}qquad t\_\{n\_r\}=r
\textbackslash{}quad\(1\leq r\leq k\).
\$\$

Then

\$\$
t\_L+U\_L=(-\textbackslash{}infty,0]\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}mathbb Z,
\$\$


\$\$
t\_R+U\_R=[k+1,\textbackslash{}infty)\textbackslash{}cap\textbackslash{}mathbb Z,
\$\$

and the singleton translates are

\$\$
\textbackslash{}\{1\textbackslash{}\},\textbackslash{}ldots,\textbackslash{}\{k\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

These sets are pairwise disjoint. The same assignment works if one or both of \$L,R\$ are absent from the finite subfamily.
However, the entire family cannot be separated. Suppose translations \$a,b,c\_n\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}mathbb Z\$ existed. Disjointness of the two rays would require

\$\$
a<b.
\$\$

For the singleton \$\textbackslash{}\{c\_n\textbackslash{}\}\$ to avoid both rays, one must have

\$\$
a<c\_n<b.
\$\$

Moreover, the \$c\_n\$ must be pairwise distinct. But the finite interval

\$\$
\textbackslash{}\{a+1,\textbackslash{}ldots,b-1\textbackslash{}\}
\$\$

contains only finitely many integers. It cannot contain all the distinct \$c\_n\$. This contradiction proves that compactness is essential for a theorem of this generality.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Why arbitrary non-open subsets cannot be allowed
\end{enumerate}
The result also fails for general subsets of a compact group, even if all the subsets are closed.
Let

\$\$
G=\textbackslash{}mathbb T=\textbackslash{}mathbb R/\textbackslash{}mathbb Z
\$\$

and choose an index set \$I\$ with cardinality strictly greater than \$|\textbackslash{}mathbb T|\$, for instance

\$\$
I=\textbackslash{}mathcal P\(\mathbb T\).
\$\$

For every \$i\textbackslash{}in I\$, put

\$\$
A\_i=\textbackslash{}\{0\textbackslash{}\}.
\$\$

Every finite subfamily is separable: simply choose finitely many distinct elements \$t\_i\textbackslash{}in\textbackslash{}mathbb T\$.
A separation of the entire family would require the singleton translates

\$\$
t\_iA\_i=\textbackslash{}\{t\_i\textbackslash{}\},
\textbackslash{}qquad i\textbackslash{}in I,
\$\$

to be pairwise disjoint. Thus \$i\textbackslash{}mapsto t\_i\$ would be an injection from \$I\$ into \$\textbackslash{}mathbb T\$, which is impossible because

\$\$
|I|=|\textbackslash{}mathcal P\(\mathbb T\)|>|\textbackslash{}mathbb T|.
\$\$

Here \$G\$ is compact Hausdorff and every \$A\_i\$ is closed, but the \$A\_i\$ are not open. Hence the openness/closed-collision condition cannot simply be discarded.

Final conclusion
The answer to Q781 is yes. For each pair \$i\textbackslash{}neq j\$, disjointness of \$t\_iU\_i\$ and \$t\_jU\_j\$ is a closed condition on the parameter tuple \$\(t_k\)\_\{k\textbackslash{}in I\}\textbackslash{}in G\textasciicircum{}I\$. The finite-separability hypothesis says that these closed conditions have the finite-intersection property. Tychonoff compactness of \$G\textasciicircum{}I\$ therefore supplies one tuple satisfying all pairwise conditions simultaneously.
